lessons.title: Lesson 1: Organising, storing and backing up drone data
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Set up a folder, naming and backup system for drone data from many farms.
This lesson builds toward: For drone data from many farms, you will set up a folder structure, naming rule, flight register and 3-2-1 backup, using Farm IDs instead of names and checking that backups open.
One mapping flight can produce hundreds of photos and several large maps. Across 200 farms and a full season, that becomes thousands of files. Without a system, data gets lost, mixed up or overwritten, and the program loses trust.
Use one clear folder structure and one naming rule for everyone: for example Program / Farm ID / Field ID / Date / raw, processed, reports. Use a Farm ID number instead of the farmer's name in file names. Keep a simple register (a spreadsheet) of every flight: date, farm ID, field, pilot, drone, files, processed yes or no.
Follow the 3-2-1 backup idea: three copies, on two different kinds of storage (for example a laptop and an external drive), with one copy in another place or a trusted cloud service. Check that backups open. Decide how long you keep raw photos, because they fill storage fast.
Step by step:
- Agree one folder structure and naming rule for the whole team.
- Give each farm and field an ID number; keep names out of file names.
- Keep a flight register spreadsheet.
- Back up: three copies, two kinds of storage, one off-site.
- Set how long raw photos are kept.
Words to know:
- Raw data: the original photos and logs straight from the drone.
- Backup: an extra copy of data kept in case the original is lost.
- Register: a list that records every flight and its files.
Try it now: Create the folder structure on your computer or phone for an example program with three farms, and start a flight register spreadsheet with the columns from this lesson. Add two example flights.
You can now organise, register and back up drone data for a multi-farm program.

check.q: Why decide how long to keep raw photos?
options: Raw photos are illegal to keep
Farmers ask for them every day
Maps cannot be made from them
check.why: Raw photos fill storage fast, so the program decides how long to keep them.

check.q: Two pilots name files differently for the same farm. What do you do?
options: Agree one folder structure and naming rule for everyone
Let each pilot use their own system
Use the farmer's name in every file
check.why: One clear folder structure and naming rule for everyone keeps data from being lost or mixed up.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Combining drone maps with GIS, satellite and farm records
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Build a GIS project that layers drone maps, field boundaries, satellite images and farm records.
This lesson builds toward: Given drone maps, field boundaries, satellite images and farm records, you will plan a GIS project that layers them and links records to fields by ID, with every layer in the same coordinate system.
GIS lets you stack different kinds of data on one map. For a program, the base layers are field boundaries (walked with a phone GPS or drawn on a drone map) and farm points. On top go drone orthomosaics and NDVI maps, free satellite images, and records such as planting date, variety, inputs and yield.
Free Sentinel-2 satellite images, viewable in the Copernicus Browser, come every few days at about 10 metres per pixel. They are too coarse for single plants but good for watching all 200 farms between drone flights. Use satellites to decide which farms need a drone visit, and drones for the detail.
Link records to fields with the Field ID, so you can ask questions like: did fields that got the drone advice yield more? QGIS can join a spreadsheet to a field layer by ID. Use the same coordinate system for every layer, or they will not line up.
Step by step:
- Make a field boundary layer with a Field ID for each field.
- Add drone maps for the fields you flew.
- Add a free satellite image of the area for the same period.
- Join your records spreadsheet to the field layer by Field ID.
- Check that every layer lines up (same coordinate system).
Words to know:
- Field boundary: a shape on a map that outlines a field.
- Sentinel-2: a pair of European satellites whose images are free; about 10 m per pixel.
- Join: linking a table to map shapes using a shared ID.
- Coordinate system: the rule a map uses to place things on the earth; layers must share one to line up.
Official sources:
- QGIS (free, open-source GIS)
- Copernicus Browser (free Sentinel satellite images)
Try it now: Open the Copernicus Browser and find your area. Then in QGIS, draw two example field boundaries, give them Field IDs, and join a small spreadsheet with planting date and variety for each.
You can now combine drone maps, satellite images, field boundaries and farm records in one GIS project.

check.q: What does GIS let you do?
options: Stack different kinds of data on one map
check.why: GIS stacks layers such as boundaries, drone maps, satellite images and records on one map.

check.q: A cooperative wants to watch all 200 farms every week but has one drone. What do you plan?
options: Use free satellite images to watch all farms and send the drone where they show a problem
check.why: Satellites watch all farms between flights; drones give the detail where it is needed.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Protecting farmers' data and getting consent
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Collect and use farmers' data lawfully, with clear consent and safe storage.
This lesson builds toward: When a program collects farmers' personal data, you will write a consent statement and data protection steps that follow the law, saying what is collected, why, who sees it, how long it is kept and that farmers can say no.
A monitoring program holds personal data: names, phone numbers, mobile money numbers, farm locations, yields and photos of homesteads. Data protection laws apply. In Kenya, the Data Protection Act 2019 is overseen by the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner (ODPC), which registers data controllers and processors. In Nigeria, the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 is overseen by the Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC). Other countries have their own laws. Check whether your organisation must register and what the law requires.
Get clear consent in the farmer's language: what you collect, why, who sees it, how long you keep it, and that they can say no or ask for it to be removed. Collect only what you need. Do not share data with buyers, lenders or others without permission.
Keep data safe: passwords on laptops and phones, limited access, and personal details stored separately from maps where you can. Farmers should get value from their own data, such as their maps and reports, not just give it away.
Step by step:
- List the personal data the program will hold.
- Check your country's data protection law and whether you must register.
- Write a short consent statement in the farmer's language.
- Collect only what you need; store it with passwords and limited access.
- Give farmers their own maps and reports.
Words to know:
- Personal data: information about a person who can be identified, such as name, phone number or farm location.
- Consent: a clear yes from a person, after they understand what will happen with their data.
- Data controller: the organisation that decides why and how personal data is used.
Official sources:
- Office of the Data Protection Commissioner (Kenya)
- Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC)
Try it now: Write a five-sentence consent statement for farmers joining a drone monitoring program, in plain words (and in a local language if you can): what you collect, why, who sees it, how long you keep it, and how to say no.
You can now collect and handle farmers' data with consent, following your country's data protection law.

check.q: In Kenya, whom does the ODPC register?
check.why: Kenya's ODPC registers data controllers and processors under the Data Protection Act 2019.

check.q: A farmer asks you to remove her data from the program. What do you do?
options: Refuse, because the data belongs to the program
Respect the request and remove it, as the consent said she could
Sell it first, then remove it
check.why: Consent tells farmers they can say no or ask for their data to be removed.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Designing a drone monitoring program

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Start with the problem and the users
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a clear program goal and list the users and what each one gets.
This lesson builds toward: For a group of farmers, you will write a program goal with a number and a date and list the users and what each gets, starting from a problem the users care about and can act on.
Many drone projects fail because they start with the drone, not the problem. Start with a problem that farmers and their partners care about and can act on: late detection of fall armyworm in a maize cooperative, uneven tea quality across estates, poor stand in cassava outgrowers, or flood damage in rice schemes.
Write one goal sentence with a number and a date, for example: By the end of the long rains 2027, find fall armyworm hotspots on 200 member farms within one week of first damage, and get confirmed advice to each affected farmer within three days.
List the users and what each gets: farmers (a map and plain advice on their phone), extension officers (where to visit first), the cooperative board (a season summary), buyers or processors (expected volumes, without personal data unless farmers agree), and the county or state agriculture office if it is a partner.
Step by step:
- Name the problem in one sentence.
- Check that users care about it and can act on it.
- Write one goal with a number and a date.
- List each user group and what it receives, and in what form.
Words to know:
- Program: an organised service that runs over time for many people, not a one-off flight.
- User: a person or group who receives and acts on the program's results.
Try it now: Write the problem, one goal sentence with a number and date, and a table of at least four user groups and what each receives for a program you could run.
You can now define a drone program's problem, goal and users clearly.

check.q: What makes a program goal clear?
options: One sentence with a number and a date
A long list of everything drones can do
check.why: A clear goal is one sentence with a number and a date, so you know when it is met.

check.q: A board member wants to buy drones first and find a use later. What do you advise?
options: Buy drones and decide next year
Start from a problem farmers care about and can act on
Ask a drone seller what to do
check.why: Many drone projects fail because they start with the drone, not the problem.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Planning people, equipment, schedule and money
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Plan the team, equipment, flight schedule and budget for one season.
This lesson builds toward: For one season of the program, you will plan the team, equipment, flight schedule and budget and how the service is paid for, including licences, one-off and running costs, and a plan for after any grant ends.
People: licensed remote pilots and observers, someone to process and analyse data, extension staff to ground-truth and advise, and a coordinator. If your program flies for others or for pay, your organisation may need an operator certificate from the aviation authority, and each pilot needs the licence your rules require.
Equipment: drones (and a spare), batteries for a full day, chargers (a solar or vehicle charging option where power is unreliable), a laptop that can process maps, storage, phones or tablets, safety gear and transport. Schedule: map the crop calendar and decide flights per farm per season; group farms by area so a team covers many in one day.
Money: list one-off costs (drones, laptop, training, licences and certificates) and running costs (staff, transport, data bundles, repairs, insurance, fees). Then decide how it is paid: a fee per acre or hectare collected by mobile money, a cooperative levy on deliveries, a buyer or processor that benefits, a government or donor grant for a start-up period. Plan for after the grant ends.
Step by step:
- List roles and the licences or certificates each needs.
- List equipment, including spares and charging.
- Draw the season schedule from the crop calendar; group farms by area.
- List one-off and running costs.
- Choose how the service is paid for, and how it continues after any grant.
Words to know:
- One-off cost: a cost paid once, such as buying a drone.
- Running cost: a cost that repeats, such as transport and staff.
- Levy: a small charge collected from members, for example per kilogram delivered.
Official sources:
- Kenya Civil Aviation Authority (KCAA): Unmanned Aircraft Systems
- Nigeria Civil Aviation Authority (NCAA): Nig.CARs 2023 Part 21, Remotely Piloted Aircraft Systems
- FAO and ITU: E-agriculture in Action: Drones for Agriculture (2018)
Try it now: For your program from Lesson 4, write a team list, an equipment list, a season schedule (which weeks you fly where) and a simple budget table of one-off and running costs with how each will be paid.
You can now plan the team, equipment, schedule and budget of a drone monitoring program.

check.q: Which is a one-off cost for a drone program?
options: Buying the drones and the laptop
check.why: Equipment such as drones and a laptop is a one-off cost; transport, data and wages are running costs.

check.q: A volunteer offers to fly for the program but has no remote pilot licence. What do you do?
options: Do not let them fly until they have the licence the rules require
Let them fly on small farms only
Let them fly if the coordinator watches
check.why: Each pilot needs the licence the country's rules require.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Measuring results and reporting
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose measures of success and report results honestly to farmers and partners.
This lesson builds toward: At the end of a season, you will choose measures of success and report results to each user, compared with a baseline and honest about what did not work.
A program is worth continuing only if it makes a difference. Choose a few measures linked to your goal: how fast problems were found, how many farmers got advice in time, how many acted on it, yield or quality compared with farms or seasons without the program, and the cost per farm.
Collect a baseline before you start (for example last season's yields or detection times), so you can compare. Ask farmers too: was the advice clear and useful, and would they pay for it? Their answers matter as much as the numbers.
Report in a form each user can use: a short message to farmers, a one-page summary with a map for the board, a fuller report for partners. Be honest about what did not work. Then improve the design for next season.
Step by step:
- Pick three to five measures linked to the goal.
- Record a baseline before the program starts.
- Collect the measures and farmer feedback during the season.
- Report in the right form for each user.
- List what to improve next season.
Words to know:
- Baseline: the situation before the program starts, used for comparison.
- Measure of success: a number that shows whether the program reached its goal.
Try it now: Final task: write your two-page program design for a cooperative of 200 smallholders: problem and goal, users, data plan with GIS and consent, team and equipment, season schedule, budget and payment model, measures of success with baseline, and reporting.
You can now measure, report and improve a drone monitoring program, and present a full program design.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Problem, goal and users Starts with the drone, or the goal has no number or date. A real problem, a goal with a number and a date, and each user with what they get. Shows the users agreed the problem, for example from a farmer meeting. Data plan No storage, naming or backup plan. Folder structure, Farm IDs, a flight register and 3-2-1 backups. Says how long raw photos are kept and who checks the backups. GIS and satellite use No GIS layers or satellite use. GIS layers listed, records linked by Field ID, and satellites used to choose where to fly. Names a question the joined data will answer, such as yield with and without advice. Consent and data protection No consent or data protection steps. Consent in the farmer's language, data minimisation, safe storage and no sharing without permission, under the right law. Checks whether the organisation must register with the data protection authority. Team, schedule and budget Missing licences, schedule or how it is paid for. Licensed team, equipment, a season flight schedule, one-off and running costs, and how the service is paid for. Shows a plan for after any grant ends. Measures and reporting No measures or baseline. A few measures linked to the goal, a baseline, and a report form for each user. Includes farmers' views on whether the advice was useful and worth paying for. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part of the design and check it again.

check.q: Which is an example of a baseline?
options: Last season's yields or detection times, recorded before you start
check.why: A baseline is the situation before the program, so results can be compared.

check.q: Farmers say the maps were accurate but the advice was hard to understand. What do you do?
options: Leave it out of the report
Report it honestly and change how advice is given next season
check.why: Be honest about what did not work, then improve the design for next season.
